title: Regional robustness narratives and escalation scripts
content:
Purpose:
This note collects short, medium, and long-form narratives plus escalation scripts for GTM and support to use when a customer experiences degraded inference capacity or region-level disruption. The aim is to give field teams ready phrases that are accurate, technically grounded, and highlight Redwood inference controls that preserve trust (routing, model variants, dedicated pools).

Audience:
- Customer success managers and account execs
- Pre-sales engineers and solutions architects
- Support tier 2/3 agents
- Product marketers drafting docs and release notes

Context and constraints:
- Customers value predictable availability and clear remediation options. They also want reassurance that their latency and cost goals are understood.
- Communications must avoid overpromising specific RTO/RPO unless documented in contract/SLA.
- Use plain-language analogies for execs, technical specifics for eng/infra contacts.

Key GTM message pillars (short):
- We design for graceful degradation: when full capacity isn’t available we automatically route to compatible variants and nearby regions to keep requests moving.
- Transparent controls: we provide per-route dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, and traceable fallbacks so you can audit changes.
- Predictable options: Dedicated capacity and reserved pools reduce exposure to noisy neighbors; private deployments give network isolation where required.

Situation brief (one-paragraph customer-facing summary):
"We observed elevated demand in the us-west region that affected some inference queues. Our platform detected the load and engaged our multi-region routing policy to rehome traffic to healthy replicas and compatible model variants with a slight latency increase. For customers on Dedicated, capacity bursts were used first; for hosted routes we applied prioritized routing and rolling fallbacks. No model outputs were altered beyond routine sampling variance. We’ll continue to monitor and will share a technical timeline and remediation actions as soon as the post-incident analysis is complete."

Incident narrative templates (ready-to-send):
1) Short (for status updates / dashboards):
"Status: Partial regional throttling detected in europe-north. Traffic is being served by eu-central and our compatibility variants; latency is +20–50ms for affected routes. No data exposure. Investigating primary root cause; next update in 60 minutes."

2) Medium (for customers impacted in multiple regions):
"What happened: An autoscaling regression in a third-party patch reduced available inference workers in eu-north while traffic spiked. How we responded: Smart routing moved requests to eu-central and us-east replicas, and we applied priority queuing for Reserved capacity customers. Impact: Some customers experienced elevated tail latency and token throughput reductions for up to 45 minutes. Mitigation: We rolled back the patch, rebalanced routing weights, and initiated a warm-up for additional replicas. Next steps: Post-incident report with timeline and mitigations will be shared within 48 hours."

3) Long (for post-incident customer email / exec summary):
"Root cause: An interaction between the autoscaler and a kernel selection heuristic on a subset of GPU instances caused worker saturation and degraded scheduling decisions. Why it mattered: Our scheduler temporarily overcommitted long-running streams, leaving insufficient slots for short conversational workloads, which increased tail latency. Why our design limited the blast radius: Smart routing, compatibility-model fallbacks, and Dedicated pool isolation kept the majority of traffic within SLA expectations. Actions taken: reversed the autoscaler change, adjusted heuristic thresholds, increased KV-cache TTL to reduce cold starts, and added an emergency autoscaler override for priority customers. Preventive measures: improved integration tests for kernel heuristics, expanded canary coverage for autoscaler changes, and an alert that triages this failure mode directly to SRE + product.

Escalation script for support -> engineering (internal):
- Subject: [P0] Regional inference saturation - {region} - impact to {customer/route}
- Body template:
  Summary: {one-line summary}
  Observable: {error rates, latency percentiles, token drop info}
  Immediate mitigation attempted: {routing changes, model variant switch, capacity burst applied}
  Business impact: {customer names, paid tiers affected, SLAs at risk}
  Ask: Please triage to serving-runtime on-call and assess whether rollback or capacity injection is required.

Priority messaging to sales / AE (script for calls):
Opening line: "We’re actively containing a localized capacity issue; I want to be transparent about what we’re seeing and what we’re doing."
Three supporting bullets:
- Contain: "We routed traffic intelligently to minimize user-visible outages and leveraged Dedicated pools where reserved capacity existed."
- Restore: "We performed targeted rollbacks and increased warm replicas to restore normal tail latency in under X hours."
- Commit: "We’ll provide a customer-specific remediation plan and timeline, plus preventive steps and options (Dedicated/reserved, multi-region pinning)."
Close with: "I’ll follow up with the RCA and a tailored proposal for reducing your exposure to this class of failure."

Region prioritization guidance (how to explain routing choices):
- Preference order: 1) Same region, warm replicas (lowest latency); 2) Nearby region with low geo-latency and compatible hardware; 3) Multi-region fallback to cheaper model variant if latency-sensitive routes permit degradation; 4) Long-haul routing to resilient pools for availability-critical workloads.
- Explain cost/latency trade-offs to customers: routing to a different region may raise egress/latency costs but preserves availability. Offer a quick decision tree: do you want to prioritize latency, consistency of model outputs, or guaranteed availability?

Competitive angle notes (how to position vs competitors during/after incidents):
- Competitor A (simple managed endpoints): they either throttle or surface errors when local capacity is exhausted. Our message: Redwood keeps traffic flowing via routing + compatible variants and provides per-route transparency so you can quantify degradation.
- Competitor B (self-hosted runtimes): strong control but heavy ops; pitch: Redwood provides avoidance of ops overhead with the same deterministic controls (Dedicated + private deployment) and SRE-backed escalation for outages.
- Competitor C (single-region SLAs): limited multi-region policy; pitch: our multi-region routing is policy-driven and observable, so you can choose failover behavior per-route.

Language dos and don’ts (for trust preservation):
- Dos: be specific about actions taken (rolled back, rerouted, warmed replicas). Acknowledge impact severity and timeline. Offer clear next steps and concrete follow-up timing.
- Don’ts: avoid vague absolutes ("no user was impacted") unless verified; avoid technical jargon with non-technical stakeholders; don’t speculate on root cause prior to triage.

Customer remediation offerings (templates to propose):
- Quick-fix: "We can pin your critical routes to Dedicated pools for predictable throughput — typically reduces incidents of this class by >90%."
- Mid-term: "Enable cross-region warm replicas for your top 5 routes and route-level canaries — we’ll help size capacity and simulate failovers."
- Long-term: "Private deployment or VPC option with regional isolation and direct KMS integration for compliance-bound workloads."

Field playbook checklist (bullet steps for responders):
- Initial 0–15m: confirm scope, enable high-level routing policy to divert non-critical traffic, notify SRE and AE teams.
- 15–60m: apply compatible-model fallbacks for tolerant routes, apply Dedicated bursts where subscribed, post status update to customers.
- 1–4h: stabilize replicas, rollback suspect infra changes, run targeted warmups of model caches.
- Post mortem: collect traces, evaluate alert gaps, produce RCA and customer-specific mitigation plan.

Examples of short trust phrases (for UI banners/emails):
- "We rerouted requests to healthy replicas to maintain availability; some requests may have slightly higher latency."
- "We applied prioritized capacity bursts for reserved customers while we remedied the root cause."

Open questions & decisions for PM/SRE:
- Thresholds: decide the latency/queue depth thresholds that should trigger automatic multi-region routing.
- Pricing: confirm whether cross-region egress for emergency routing is billable or absorbed by Redwood for customers with SLA.
- Alerts: define the alert that must notify GTM immediately (not just on-call) for incidents that may affect >5% of requests for >15m.

Appendix: Quick tech primer to support messages
- Smart routing: policy layer that weights healthy endpoints by latency, cost, and customer tier; supports canary weights and emergency overrides.
- Compatibility variants: compiled model variants differing in kernel choices or quantization that are functionally compatible for fallback when exact model instance is unavailable.
- KV-cache warmups: pre-populating prefix caches to reduce cold start latency for conversational flows.
- Dedicated pools: reserved GPU capacity with pre-warmed workers for predictable throughput.

Notes from last market test (internal):
- In our multi-region simulation with a synthetic spike, routing + compatible variants kept 92% of requests served within a 10% latency delta; naive throttling would have produced 18% errors. Share these numbers as "internal benchmark" but do not promise identical results for customers.

End of doc.

Author notes: keep this doc lean and update with actual incident case studies — we should replace placeholders with real RCA facts before sharing externally.
